Printed by Na vneet Education Limited, Dantali, Gujarat. 2626 CTP (20/9/25) Study Tips Dear Students, The syllabus must be nearing completion. The coming days are for self- study and to make an effective study plan. So far, during the year ‘Navneet Digests’ have helped you in your studies. From now onwards start your preparations with the help of ‘21 Most Likely Question Sets’ which are based on the latest paper pattern. Y ou will know about the important questions from examination point of view and guidance on how to write accurate answers. How will you prepare for your Board exam in this limited but crucial time period? 1. F irst of all carefully analyse the Model Question Paper and all types of questions based on the latest paper pattern. 2. K eep in mind that Q. 1., Q. 2. and Q. 3. are objective type questions. The questions like fill in the blanks, match the pairs, identify incorrect pair, identify odd man out, answer in one sentence, differentiate between, complete the chain, etc. will be asked in these questions. By thorough revision, you can score full marks in these questions. 3. Q. 4. will be a map based question. A separate map will be provided for map filling. For map reading, a map will be given in question paper. Q. 5. will be a question of give reasons. Q. 6. will be a diagram/graph based question. By thorough practice, you can score full marks in all these questions. 4. Q. 7. will be Long answer question. You can answer this question with suitable diagrams wherever necessary. 5. By careful analyses of the Solved Board’s Question Paper of July 2024 and Board’s Question Paper of July 2025 given for practice, you will realise that your basic concepts of every chapter of Geography must be very clear. 6. Speed, accuracy and writing practice are also essential to master the art of answering the questions. 7. Solve all the question papers given for practice in Navneet Practice Papers : Std. X. It will surely help you to familiarise yourself with questions of different types and boost your confidence. ALL THE BEST FOR YOUR FURTHER STUDIES AND THE FORTHCOMING BOARD EXAMINATION.

8 NAVNEET 21 M. L. Q. SETS : GEOGRAPHY – STD. X Answers (1) (1) India is spread in the Northern and Eastern Hemisphere of the earth. It is located in the Southern part of the Asian continent. (2) The latitudinal extent of the mainland of India is from 8°4′N latitude to 37°6 ′N latitude. The longitudinal extent of India is from 68°7′E longitude to 97°25′E longitude. (3) Indira Point is the southernmost point of India’s territory. It is located on Nicobar island at 6°45 ′ latitude. (4) The Tropic of Cancer passes through the centre of India. (2) (1) The Great Escarpment is the smallest physiographical region of Brazil. From Sao Paulo to Porto Alegre, the height of Brazilian Highlands/ Plateau decreases remarkably leading to the formation of the Great Escarpment. The Great Escarpment demarcates the eastern side of the Brazilian Highlands/Plateau. (2) The altitude of Brazilian Highlands is approximately 790 m in the region of the Great Escarpment. In other regions, its height decreases gradually. (3) The nature and the slope of the Great Escarpment affects the climatic conditions of Brazil. It acts as a barrier to the southeast Trade winds. (4) The Great Escarpment leads to heavy rains in the Brazilian coastal areas and it also gives rise to the rain shadow area to the northeast of the Brazilian Highlands. This rain shadow area is known as ‘Drought Quadrilateral’. (3) (1) The Indian Ocean plays an important role in the formation of southwest monsoon winds.

Q. 5 Give geographical reasons : (Any two) 6 (1) India is a major trading partner for other countries of the world. (Ch. 2) (2) Brazil does not receive snowfall. (Ch. 4) (3) Settlements are sparse in Northeastern Brazil. (Ch. 7) (4) Telecom industry has become one of the fastest growing sector in India. (Ch. 9) Answers (1) (1) India is one of the major developing countries. (2) After independence, many economic reforms took place in India. These reforms increased the rate of economic development in India. (3) The proportion of working population (youth) is comparatively high in India. Therefore, India is a major developing country of the world.

BOARD’S QUESTION PAPER : JULY 2024 (With Full Solution …) 13 (2) (1) Snowfall generally occurs in the temperate and polar zone due to polar winds. It also occurs in the mountainous and hilly regions of high altitudes. (2) Brazil is not located in polar region. Most of its part is located in the tropical zone. (3) There are no mountainous regions in Brazil. Therefore, snowfall doesn’t always occur in Brazil. (3) (1) Northeastern Brazil is a rain shadow region. (2) The amount of annual average rainfall in this region is only 600 mm. Therefore, this region is considered as drought-prone. (3) Due to scanty rainfall, agriculture and other industries are not well-developed in this region. Therefore, settlements are sparse in northeastern Brazil. (4) (1) India has made progress in the field of information technology and communication. (2) The electronic devices such as computer, mobiles, internet, satellites, etc. are widely used in India. (3) Today, India is one of the largest countries using smartphones and internet for wide reach of communication. (4) With the development of its own satellite, India has proved itself in the field of modern communication. Therefore, telecom industry has become one of the fastest growing sector in India. (3 marks each for any two sub-questions. Total 6 marks.) Note : (1) Q. 6. will be given with internal options. (2) Students will have to write either (A) OR (B). (3) For Q. 6. Q. 7 Answer the following questions in detail : (Any two) 8 (1) What is field visit? What precautions you will take when you visit a sea coast? (Ch. 1) (2) Write detailed information on Himalayan Mountains. (Ch. 3) (3) What are the major causes of degradation of forest in Brazil and India? (Ch. 5) Answers (1) (A) Meaning : (1) Geography can be studied better by observation. (2) The entire earth is considered as the laboratory for geography. (3) The study of entire earth is not possible for field visit. (4) So a small specific area is selected of which we study the natural and cultural features is called as field visit. (B) We will take of the following precautions when we visit a seashore : (1) While going for a field visit to a seashore we will confirm the timings of high and low tides. (2) We will take a local guide while visiting a seashore or a mountainous region. We will not go to an unknown place.

BOARD’S QUESTION PAPER : JULY 2024 (With Full Solution …) 17 (3) We will avoid taking a selfie near risky areas like sea cliffs or any other places in the deep sea. (4) We will not enter into deep sea for swimming. (5) We will keep the seashore clean. We will not litter. (6) We will follow all the instructions given by our teacher and written on the boards near the seashore. (2) (1) Himalayas is one of the young fold mountains in the world. It extends from Pamir Knot in Tajikistan in the west to the east. Himalayas is one of the major mountain systems of the continent of Asia. (2) In India, Himalayas extends from Jammu and Kashmir in the north to Arunachal Pradesh in the northeast. Himalayas as well as many other parallel mountain ranges get included in Himalayas mountain system. Shivalik is the southernmost mountain range of Himalayas. It is the youngest mountain range of Himalayas. (3) As we move from Shivalik range in the south to the north, we come across Lesser Himalayas, Greater Himalayas and Trans Himalayan ranges respectively. These ranges are young to old respectively. (4) The Himalayan mountain ranges can also be divided from the west to the east into Western Himalayas (or Kashmir Himalaya), Central Himalaya (or Kumaun Himalayas) and Eastern Himalaya (Assam Himalayas). (3) The following are the major causes of degradation of forests in Brazil and India : (1) In Brazil, as well as in India, there is shortage of land for human settlements. (2) For obtaining the space for settlements, trees are cut down on a large scale in both the countries.

18 NAVNEET 21 M. L. Q. SETS : GEOGRAPHY – STD. X (3) Roka type of farming is practised in Brazil. Zoom agriculture is practised in India. In these types of farming, the forest area is cleared on a large scale for the agricultural activities. These islands are divided into the coastal islands and the marine islands. (2) Most of the coastal islands of Brazil are formed due to depositional work of Amazon river and its tributaries. The islands near the eastern coast of Brazil that are in South Atlantic Ocean are coral islands. These islands are called atolls. (3) Most of Marine islands were a part of the mainland of Brazil. These islands are located in the Atlantic Ocean and nearly 300 km away from the mainland of Brazil. (4) Most of marine islands of Brazil are rocky. These islands are the tops of the submerged mountains. (9) The characteristics of the Western Ghats. Ans. The characteristics of the Western Ghats are as follows : (1) The Western Ghats is a mountain range that runs north to south parallel to the Western Coast of the Indian peninsula. (2) It demarcates the western side of Deccan plateau. Many peninsular rivers like Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri have their source in Western Ghats.

QUESTION SET 14 : WRITE SHORT NOTES 59 (3) The Western Ghats is not a single mountain like a wall. It includes series of ranges. At some places, it has regions of very low altitude too. (4) The Western Ghats separate the westward flowing rivers meeting to Arabian Sea from the eastward flowing rivers meeting the Bay of Bengal. (10) Amazon river basin. Ans. (1) Amazon river basin is the largest plain land of Brazil. It lies in the northern part of Brazil. The slope of Amazon river basin is to the east. (2) The width of Amazon river basin is the maximum, i.e. nearly 1300 km in the west. Its width is the minimum, i.e. 240 km where the Guiana Highlands and Brazilian Highlands come closer. (3) As the Amazon river approaches the Atlantic Ocean, the width of Amazon river basin/plains increases. (4) Amazon river basin/plains is covered by the evergreen tropical rainforests. Most of the area of Amazon river basin is inaccessible due to dense undergrowth and frequent flooding. (11) The Indian peninsula. Ans. (1) The Indian peninsula lies to the south of North Indian Plains. This region tapers towards the Indian Ocean. (2) Many plateaus and hill ranges are included in the Indian peninsula. The Aravalis range is located in the north of the Indian peninsula. It is the oldest mountain range in the Indian peninsula. (3) The Indian peninsula also includes a series of plateaus bordering the Plains. Maharashtra Plateau, Karnataka-Telangana Plateau, Chhota Nagpur Plateau, etc. are the main plateaus in this region. (4) Vindhyas and Satpuda ranges are located in the central part of the Indian peninsula. It also includes mountainous/hilly regions of the Western Ghats in the west and the Eastern Ghats in the east. (12) Guyana Highlands. Ans. (1) The main region of the Guyana Highlands is in Venezuela. Guyana Highlands extents from the west to French Guiana in the east.

The height of this peak is nearly 3014 m. (4) Guyana Highlands and Brazilian Highlands together form the core of the continent of South America. CHAPTER 4 : CLIMATE (13) Retreating monsoon. (March ’24) Ans. (1) The southwest monsoon winds flowing from the mainland of India are obstructed by the Himalayan ranges in the north resulting their return journey backward towards the Indian Ocean. (2) These winds blowing from northeast to southwest direction again brings monsoon to Indian Peninsula. This monsoon is called as retreating monsoon. CHAPTER 5 : NATURAL VEGETATION AND WILDLIFE (14) The evergreen forests in India. Ans. (1) The evergreen forests in India are found in the regions receiving abundant sunlight and annual average rainfall more than 2000 mm. These forests are found in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Western Ghats, the coastline of peninsular India and the Assam region in the north-east. (2) The trees like mahogany, rosewood, rubber, sandalwood, etc. are found in the evergreen forests in India. Various types of creepers are also found in these forests. (3) The trees from evergreen forests have broad and green leaves. Their wood is found to be hard, heavy and durable. (4) Many species of vegetation and wildlife is found in evergreen forests in India. (15) Wildlife in India. Ans. (1) India is gifted with rich and diversified wildlife. India is the only country in the world that has tigers as well as lions. (2) Elephants are found in the hot and humid forests in the

QUESTION SET 14 : WRITE SHORT NOTES 61 southern part of India. Assam is famous for one-horned rhinoceroses. They are found in swampy and marshy lands of Assam. Wild ass and camels are commonly found in arid desert lands in India. Snow leopards and yaks are found in the snow capped northern regions of Himalayan range. (3) Indian bisons, deer, antelopes, monkeys are the animals seen in peninsular region of India. Turtles, crocodiles and gharials are seen in the rivers, estuaries and western and eastern coastal regions of India. (4) Peacocks, Indian bustard, kingfishers, peasants, ducks, parakeets, cranes, pigeons, etc. are the major birds seen in various parts of India. (16) Himalayan forests in India. Ans. (1) The forests in Himalayan range are known as Himalayan forests. Himalayan forests are classified into three types on the basis of altitude. (2) The areas at higher altitude in Himalayan range are often covered with snow. In summer, the snow from this region starts melting leading to growth of seasonal flowing trees. (3) The areas at medium altitude in the Himalayan range are covered with the forests having the coniferous trees like pine, deodar, fir, etc. These trees have needle-shaped leaves. These leaves allows for snow to easily glide off the branches. (4) The areas at low altitude in the Himalayan range, i.e. at the foothills of Himalayan range, mixed forests are found. Coniferous as well as deciduous types of forests are found in this region. Sal trees are seen in greater quantities in most of these forests. (17) Deciduous forests of India. (March ’24) Ans. (1) Deciduous forests are found in India in the areas receiving rainfall between 1000 mm and 2000 mm. (2) Deciduous type of vegetation is characterised by trees that shed their leaves during dry/summer season. (3) Trees like Teak, Bamboo, Banyan, Peepal, etc. are found in deciduous forests in India. (4) Most of the forest area of India is covered by deciduous forests.

CHAPTER 3 : PHYSIOGRAPHY AND DRAINAGE (4) (Most of the) Himalayan rivers are perennial in nature. (Sept. ’21; March ’25) Ans. (1) Most of the Himalayan rivers originate in the snow covered southern heights of the Himalayan range. (2) These rivers are well fed by rains during the rainy season through the southwesterly monsoon winds. (3) These rivers are also fed by the melting of snow during summer. Therefore, most of the Himalayan rivers are perennial in nature. (5) There are fewer natural ports on the eastern coast of India. (March ’19; Nov. ’20; July ’22 – ’23) Ans. (1) The eastern coast of India is formed due to the depositional work of eastward flowing rivers meeting the Bay of Bengal. (2) Most of the western coast of India is a coast of submergence. On the other hand eastern coast of India is a coast of emergence. As its effect, sea is deeper in the west than sea on the eastern coast. (3) Westward flowing rivers meeting the Arabian Sea form estuaries at many places on the western coast. On the other hand, eastward flowing rivers meeting the Bay of Bengal form deltas at many places on the eastern coast. As its effect, it becomes difficult for ships to reach the east coast covered with sediments. Therefore, there are fewer natural ports on the eastern coast of India. (6) There are no west-flowing rivers in Brazil. Ans. (1) Most of the rivers in Brazil originate from the Brazilian Highlands. (2) The altitude of Brazilian Highlands gradually decreases from the south to the north and from the west to the east. As its effect, most of the rivers in Brazil flow towards the northern and eastern direction.

(1) India receives most of its precipitation from the southwest monsoon winds. These winds enter the mainland of India from the southern regions and gradually flow towards the northern regions of India. (2) These winds are obstructed by the Himalayan ranges in the north. As its effect, these winds start their return journey and start flowing backward towards the Indian Ocean. (3) In their return journey, these winds blow from northeast to southwest direction. As its effect, these winds bring retreating monsoon in India. Thus, India receives precipitation from the northeast monsoon winds too. (9) Snowfall doesn’t always occur in Brazil. (Nov. ’20) Ans. CHAPTER 4 : CLIMATE (16) Explain the importance of Himalayas and the Indian Ocean with respect to the climate of India. (Sept. ’21) Ans. The importance of Himalayas and the Indian Ocean with respect to the climate of India can be explained as follows : (1) The Indian Ocean and Himalayan ranges play an important role in formation of southeast monsoon winds. (2) In summers, the temperature in Punjab Plains and the Thar desert is found to be high. As its effect, the areas of low pressure are developed. (3) On the other hand, the areas of high pressure are found in the Indian Ocean. This leads to formation and flowing of southeast monsoon winds from the Indian Ocean to the mainland of India. (4) These winds are moisture-laden and so they bring rainfall in India. (5) Himalayas saves India by obstructing the passage of very cold winds from the north into India in winter. (6) The southwest monsoon winds flow from the south to the north and reaches towards the Himalayas. (7) These winds are obstructed by the Himalayas. Due to obstruction, these winds change their direction and start flowing from the northeast to the Indian Ocean. (8) The return journey of these winds bring the retreating monsoon in peninsular region of India. (17) Compare the climates of Brazil and India. (July ’19; March ’22) Ans. Therefore, the deciduous type of vegetation occupies most of India.

122 NAVNEET 21 M. L. Q. SETS : GEOGRAPHY – STD. X (28) Where do you find thorny and shrub vegetation in India? Why? Ans. (1) Thorny and shrub vegetation is found in the state of Rajasthan and in the central part of peninsula. (2) Most of region of Rajasthan and the central part of peninsula is included in a rain shadow area. (3) The annual average rainfall received by these region is less than 500 mm. (4) Thorny and shrub like vegetation is mainly grown in the areas experiencing hot summers and receiving less than 500 mm of rainfall. Therefore, thorny and shrub vegetation is found in Rajasthan and the peninsula. CHAPTER 6 : POPULATION (29) Giving examples, correlate climate and population distribution. Ans. (1) Climate and population distribution are closely related. The sparse distribution of population is found in the regions having heavy or scarce rainfall or too high or too low temperature. (2) For example, in India, the sparse distribution of population is found in snow covered regions in Himalayan range as well as hot Thar desert. Similarly, in Brazil, the sparse distribution of population is found in the Amazon river basin receiving heavy rainfall. (3) The dense distribution of population is found in the regions having average amount of rainfall and moderate temperature. (4) For example, in India, the dense distribution of population is found in Ganga plains having average amount of rainfall and moderate temperature. Similarly, in Brazil, the dense distribution of population is found near southeastern coastal areas having average amount of rainfall and moderate temperature. (30) Write a note on population growth rate in India and Brazil. Ans. (A) Population growth rate in India : (1) In India, population growth rate was between 2 per cent to 2.3 per cent till 1971.

QUESTION SET 20 : ANSWER THE FOLLOWING ... 123 (2) From 1971 to 1991, the growth rate of population in India stabilised with 2.3 per cent. (3) From 1991, the growth rate of population in India is slowly declining. (4) In 2011, the growth rate of population in India was 1.7 per cent. (5) Due to steeply falling death rate and slowly falling birth rate, the population of India is still growing. (B) Population growth rate in Brazil : (1) From 1970 to 2010, the growth rate of population in Brazil had reduced considerably. (2) In 1970, the growth rate of population in Brazil was 3 per cent. On the contrary, in 2010, the growth rate of population in Brazil is only 0.3 per cent. (3) Extremely limited population growth rate of Brazil indicates that population of Brazil may not increase considerably in the next two decades. (31) Correlate climate of southeastern coastal region of Brazil and population distribution. Ans. (1) Temperate type of climate is found in the southeastern coastal region of Brazil. (2) Mild and humid climate, average amount of rainfall, fertile soil and availability of resources have helped in flourishing agriculture and industries in the southeastern coastal region of Brazil. (3) These favourable factors have led to dense distribution of population in the southeastern coastal regions of Brazil. (4) According to Census 2010, the density of population in the southeastern coastal region (in the states of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro) was the maximum, i.e. more than 300 persons per sq. km. (32) Correlate life expectancy and social development. Ans. (1) Increase in life expectancy indicates increase in social development of a country. (2) Availability of medical facilities, advancement in medical sciences, availability of nutritious food, etc. factors help in increasing life expectancy.

124 NAVNEET 21 M. L. Q. SETS : GEOGRAPHY – STD. X (3) Compared to developed countries, life expectancy in developing countries is very less. Due to progress in the social and economic development in developing countries, the life expectancy in developing countries is gradually increasing. (4) In India, in 1960, the life expectancy was only 41 years. On the contrary, in 2016 it was 68 years. This increase in life expectancy indicates increase in social development in India. CHAPTER 7 : HUMAN SETTLEMENTS (33) Write a comparative note on urbanisation in Brazil and India. (March ’23) Ans. (1) In Brazil, the rate of urbanisation is comparatively higher and in India, the rate of urbanisation is comparatively lower. (2) In 2011, the rate of urbanisation in India was only 31.2 per cent. On the other hand in 2010, the rate of urbanisation in Brazil was 84.6 per cent. (3) In India, the rate of urbanisation increased from 18 per cent in 1961 to 31.2 per cent in 2011. (4) In Brazil, the rate of urbanisation increased from 47.1 per cent in 1960 to 84.6 per cent in 2010. (5) In India, the rate of urbanisation has increased continuously from 1961 to 2011. (6) In India, the rate of urbanisation has increased with fluctuating rate from 1961 to 2011. (7) In Brazil, the rate of urbanisation has increased from 1960 to 2010. (8) In Brazil, though the rate of urbanisation has increased from 1960 to 2010, it has increased by diminishing rate. (34) Write in detail about human settlements in India. Ans. (1) There exists variety in the patterns of human settlements in India. (2) Variety in climatic conditions, availability of water, slope of land, fertility of land, level of development, etc. variety in human settlements is seen. (3) In the river basins of Ganga, Narmada, Godavari, etc, nucleated settlements are seen in India.

QUESTION SET 20 : ANSWER THE FOLLOWING ... 125 (4) On the other hand, in the hot and arid area of Thar desert, scattered human settlements are seen in India. (5) In India, nucleated settlements are seen in North Indian Plains and eastern coastal region. (6) Dense human settlements are also seen in plateau region of Narmada valley, paddy lands in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Vindhyan Plateau and many other cultivable regions. (7) Dispersed settlements are also seen in dense forest covered regions, tribal parts of Central India, western and southern Rajasthan, Himalayan slopes and land of uneven topography. (8) In India, compared to urban settlements, rural settlements are found in greater numbers. (35) Write a note on the urban population in India. Ans. (1) In India, urban population is seen to be comparatively more in the states located in the central and southern part of India. Urban population is seen to comparatively low in states located in northern and northeast parts of India. (2) The states of Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Haryana and Punjab located in the northern part of India as well as the states of Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Tripura located in the northeast part has only 0 to 40 per cent urban population. (3) The union territories of Chandigarh and NCT of Delhi located in the northern part of India has 81 to 100 per cent of urban population. (4) The state of Gujarat located in the central part of India has 41 to 80 per cent of urban population. (5) The union territories of Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli has 41 to 80 per cent of urban population. (6) The states of Maharashtra, Goa, Telangana, Kerala and Tamil Nadu located in the southern part of India has 41 to 80 per cent of urban population. (7) The union territory of Lakshadweep Islands has 61 to 80 per cent of urban population. The union territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands has 21 to 40 per cent of urban population.

126 NAVNEET 21 M. L. Q. SETS : GEOGRAPHY – STD. X (8) In India, the percentage of urban population is continuously rising. CHAPTER 8 : ECONOMY AND OCCUPATIONS (36) What are the similarities and differences in the fishing activities in Brazil and India? (March ’19; Sept. ’21) Ans. (A) The similarities in the fishing activities in Brazil and India : (1) The marine fishing is practised in Brazil as well as India. (2) The fishing is carried out on a large scale in salt water in Brazil and India. (B) The differences in the fishing activities in Brazil and India : (1) In India, fresh water fishing is carried on at many places in rivers, canals, irrigation canals, tanks, ponds, lakes, etc. On the other hand, in Brazil, fresh water fishing is carried on a small scale due to rigid topography, dense forests and speedy discharge of rivers. (2) Plankton is located on a large scale at the confluence of warm and cold ocean currents. Plankton provide a crucial source of food to fish. Due to confluence of hot and cold ocean currents near the eastern coast, fishing is well-developed in Brazil. On the other hand, though there is no such confluence of hot and ocean currents, fishing is developed in India due to many other favourable factors. (37) Why has mining not developed in the western part of Brazil? Ans. (1) There are comparatively less number of mineral deposits in the western part of Brazil. (2) Most of the western part of Brazil is covered by the Amazon river basin. There are evergreen dense rainforests in this areas. Due to dense forests this area has become inaccessible. As its effect, there are natural limitations on the use and exploitation of mineral resources available in this areas. (3) The density of human settlement is very low in the western part of Brazil. Thus, the demand for minerals in this part is comparatively low.

QUESTION SET 20 : ANSWER THE FOLLOWING ... 127 (4) Similarly, transport facilities are poorly developed in this areas. Therefore, mining has not developed in the western part of Brazil. (38) Write information about agriculture occupation in India. Ans. The information of agriculture in India can be given with the help of the following points : (1) Features : The features of agriculture in India are as follows : (1) Agriculture is one of the traditional occupations in India. (2) Nearly 60 per cent of land of India is under cultivation. (3) Most of the agriculture in India is of subsistence nature. (4) Compared to Brazil, the contribution of agriculture in Gross Domestic Product is high. (5) Compared to Brazil, the percentage of population of total population engaged in agriculture is high. (2) The factors promoting a strong base : Extensive plains, fertile soils, long growing seasons, variety in climate, etc. are the factors promoting a strong base for the development of agriculture in India. (3) Main crops grown : Rice, wheat, sorghum, millets, maize, etc. food crops, tea, coffee, cotton, sugarcane, rubber, jute, etc. cash crops and variety of spices, fruits and vegetables are grown on a large scale in India. (4) Foreign exchange : The agricultural produce like spices, mangoes, grapes, apples, vegetables, etc. are exported from India in world market. As its effect, agricultural produce helps in earning foreign exchange.

CHAPTER 3 : PHYSIOGRAPHY AND DRAINAGE (4) (Most of the) Himalayan rivers are perennial in nature. (Sept. ’21; March ’25) Ans. (1) Most of the Himalayan rivers originate in the snow covered southern heights of the Himalayan range. (2) These rivers are well fed by rains during the rainy season through the southwesterly monsoon winds. (3) These rivers are also fed by the melting of snow during summer. Therefore, most of the Himalayan rivers are perennial in nature. (5) There are fewer natural ports on the eastern coast of India. (March ’19; Nov. ’20; July ’22 – ’23) Ans. (1) The eastern coast of India is formed due to the depositional work of eastward flowing rivers meeting the Bay of Bengal. (2) Most of the western coast of India is a coast of submergence. On the other hand eastern coast of India is a coast of emergence. As its effect, sea is deeper in the west than sea on the eastern coast. (3) Westward flowing rivers meeting the Arabian Sea form estuaries at many places on the western coast. On the other hand, eastward flowing rivers meeting the Bay of Bengal form deltas at many places on the eastern coast. As its effect, it becomes difficult for ships to reach the east coast covered with sediments. Therefore, there are fewer natural ports on the eastern coast of India. (6) There are no west-flowing rivers in Brazil. Ans. (1) Most of the rivers in Brazil originate from the Brazilian Highlands. (2) The altitude of Brazilian Highlands gradually decreases from the south to the north and from the west to the east. As its effect, most of the rivers in Brazil flow towards the northern and eastern direction.

The Gujarat coast is relatively broader, but it, too, has small and narrow coastal plains. (2) The Konkan coast is full of spurs extending from the Western Ghats right up to the western coastline. It is rocky, having no vast plains. (3) The Malabar coast is characterised by sand dunes, lagoons and backwaters. It, too, does not have any fast plain. Thus, the western coast does not have vast extending plain lands. CHAPTER 4 : CLIMATE (8) India receives precipitation from the northeast monsoon winds too. (Nov. ’20; March ’23) Ans. (1) India receives most of its precipitation from the southwest monsoon winds. These winds enter the mainland of India from the southern regions and gradually flow towards the northern regions of India. (2) These winds are obstructed by the Himalayan ranges in the north. As its effect, these winds start their return journey and start flowing backward towards the Indian Ocean. (3) In their return journey, these winds blow from northeast to southwest direction. As its effect, these winds bring retreating monsoon in India. Thus, India receives precipitation from the northeast monsoon winds too. (9) Snowfall doesn’t always occur in Brazil. (Nov. ’20) Ans. Therefore, vegetation is scarce in the high altitude of Himalayas.

(B) The Indian Islands : (1) Lakshadweep Islands of India : (1) Lakshadweep Islands is a group of islands of India located in the Arabian Sea. (2) Lakshadweep Islands are to the southwest of the mainland of India. They are far away from the western coastline of India. (3) Most of the islands in Lakshadweep are atoll islands. (4) Barren Island from Andaman group has the only active volcano in India. (12) Explain the characteristics of the North Indian Plains. (March ’22) Ans. The characteristics of the North Indian Plains are as follows : (1) A flat low-lying area is located in the north of India. This region is known as the North Indian Plains. (2) The North Indian Plains lie between Himalayan Mountain in

114 NAVNEET 21 M. L. Q. SETS : GEOGRAPHY – STD. X the north and the Peninsula in the south. It extends from the states of Rajasthan and Punjab in the west to Assam in the east. (3) The North Indian Plains are divided into three parts. (4) The low-lying area to the east of the Aravalis is known as Ganga plains. It slopes to the east. (5) The delta of Ganga-Brahmaputra rivers extents in the state of West Bengal in India and Bangladesh. This region is known as Sunderbans. Sunderbans is the largest delta region in the world. (6) The western part of the North Indian Plains is occupied by desert. It is known as Thar Desert or Marusthali. The state of Rajasthan is occupied by Thar Desert. The characteristics of the highlands of Brazil are as follows : (1) The southern part of Brazil is occupied by an extensive plateau. It is known as Brazilian Highlands or Brazilian Shield or Brazilian Plateau. (2) The height of regions to the east and south of Brazilian Highlands is nearly 1000 m. In other parts, its altitude is between 500 m to 1000 m. (3) The Brazilian highlands slopes to the north. The slopes of highlands are not very steep. (4) Many rivers originate and flow from the northern slopes of the highlands of Brazil. (5) Many tributaries of Amazon flow through this region. These rivers flows from Brazil and enter Argentina.

(4) Generally, a network of distributaries is seen at the mouth of river. But due to lack of the deposition of sediments, a dense network of distributaries are not seen at the mouth of Amazon river. CHAPTER 4 : CLIMATE (16) Explain the importance of Himalayas and the Indian Ocean with respect to the climate of India. (Sept. ’21) Ans. The importance of Himalayas and the Indian Ocean with respect to the climate of India can be explained as follows : (1) The Indian Ocean and Himalayan ranges play an important role in formation of southeast monsoon winds. (2) In summers, the temperature in Punjab Plains and the Thar desert is found to be high. As its effect, the areas of low pressure are developed. (3) On the other hand, the areas of high pressure are found in the Indian Ocean. This leads to formation and flowing of southeast monsoon winds from the Indian Ocean to the mainland of India. (4) These winds are moisture-laden and so they bring rainfall in India. (5) Himalayas saves India by obstructing the passage of very cold winds from the north into India in winter. (6) The southwest monsoon winds flow from the south to the north and reaches towards the Himalayas. (7) These winds are obstructed by the Himalayas. Due to obstruction, these winds change their direction and start flowing from the northeast to the Indian Ocean. (8) The return journey of these winds bring the retreating monsoon in peninsular region of India. (17) Compare the climates of Brazil and India. (July ’19; March ’22) Ans. The climates of Brazil and India can be compared with the help of the following points :

(20) What could be the reasons behind the flowing of winds from different directions towards Brazil? Ans. The following could be the reasons behind the flowing of winds from different directions towards Brazil : (1) The equator passes through the northern part of Brazil. The low pressure belt is found near equatorial region in Brazil. (2) The winds from high pressure belt from southern and northern hemisphere flow towards this region in Brazil. (21) Correlate northeast and southeast trade winds and rainfall with reference to obstruction in their way. Ans. (1) The Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands obstructs the northeast and southeast trade winds. (2) As its effect, these winds move upwards along the slopes of the Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands. (3) At higher altitude, the condensation process takes place and windward side receives more rain. (4) Thus, the windward side of the Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands receive abundant rainfall and the rain shadow region is found to the other side. (22) Give information about Drought Quadrilateral in Brazil. Ans. (1) The Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands obstructs the trade winds flowing in southeast and northeast from the Atlantic Ocean. (2) Due to this obstruction, it rains heavily in the windward side of the Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands, i.e. in the eastern coastal region of Brazil. (3) The amount of annual average rainfall in the eastern coastal region of Brazil is nearly 1200 mm. (4) The winds that reach the top of the Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands become dry. The capacity of holding moisture of these winds increases. (5) As its effect it rains less to the leeward side of the Great Escarpment and the Brazilian Highlands. (6) Thus, the northeast part of Brazil receives the minimum rainfall. (7) The amount of annual average rainfall is only nearly 600 mm in this region. This region is a rain shadow region. (8) It is known as ‘Drought Quadrilateral’. The higher temperature is found in this region.

Therefore, thorny and shrub vegetation is found in Rajasthan and the peninsula. CHAPTER 6 : POPULATION (29) Giving examples, correlate climate and population distribution. Ans. (1) Climate and population distribution are closely related. The sparse distribution of population is found in the regions having heavy or scarce rainfall or too high or too low temperature. (2) For example, in India, the sparse distribution of population is found in snow covered regions in Himalayan range as well as hot Thar desert. Similarly, in Brazil, the sparse distribution of population is found in the Amazon river basin receiving heavy rainfall. (3) The dense distribution of population is found in the regions having average amount of rainfall and moderate temperature. (4) For example, in India, the dense distribution of population is found in Ganga plains having average amount of rainfall and moderate temperature. Similarly, in Brazil, the dense distribution of population is found near southeastern coastal areas having average amount of rainfall and moderate temperature. CHAPTER 7 : HUMAN SETTLEMENTS (33) Write a comparative note on urbanisation in Brazil and India. (March ’23) Ans. (1) In Brazil, the rate of urbanisation is comparatively higher and in India, the rate of urbanisation is comparatively lower. (2) In 2011, the rate of urbanisation in India was only 31.2 per cent. (1) There exists variety in the patterns of human settlements in India. (2) Variety in climatic conditions, availability of water, slope of land, fertility of land, level of development, etc. variety in human settlements is seen. (3) In the river basins of Ganga, Narmada, Godavari, etc, nucleated settlements are seen in India.

QUESTION SET 20 : ANSWER THE FOLLOWING ... 125 (4) On the other hand, in the hot and arid area of Thar desert, scattered human settlements are seen in India. (6) Dense human settlements are also seen in plateau region of Narmada valley, paddy lands in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Vindhyan Plateau and many other cultivable regions. (7) Dispersed settlements are also seen in dense forest covered regions, tribal parts of Central India, western and southern Rajasthan, Himalayan slopes and land of uneven topography. (8) In India, compared to urban settlements, rural settlements are found in greater numbers. (35) Write a note on the urban population in India. Ans. Urban population is seen to comparatively low in states located in northern and northeast parts of India. (2) The states of Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Haryana and Punjab located in the northern part of India as well as the states of Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Tripura located in the northeast part has only 0 to 40 per cent urban population. (3) The union territories of Chandigarh and NCT of Delhi located in the northern part of India has 81 to 100 per cent of urban population. (4) The state of Gujarat located in the central part of India has 41 to 80 per cent of urban population. (5) The union territories of Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli has 41 to 80 per cent of urban population. (6) The states of Maharashtra, Goa, Telangana, Kerala and Tamil Nadu located in the southern part of India has 41 to 80 per cent of urban population. CHAPTER 8 : ECONOMY AND OCCUPATIONS (36) What are the similarities and differences in the fishing activities in Brazil and India? (March ’19; Sept. ’21) Ans. (A) The similarities in the fishing activities in Brazil and India : (1) The marine fishing is practised in Brazil as well as India. (2) The fishing is carried out on a large scale in salt water in Brazil and India. (B) The differences in the fishing activities in Brazil and India : (1) In India, fresh water fishing is carried on at many places in rivers, canals, irrigation canals, tanks, ponds, lakes, etc. On the other hand, in Brazil, fresh water fishing is carried on a small scale due to rigid topography, dense forests and speedy discharge of rivers. (2) Plankton is located on a large scale at the confluence of warm and cold ocean currents. Plankton provide a crucial source of food to fish. Due to confluence of hot and cold ocean currents near the eastern coast, fishing is well-developed in Brazil. On the other hand, though there is no such confluence of hot and ocean currents, fishing is developed in India due to many other favourable factors. (37) Why has mining not developed in the western part of Brazil? Ans. (1) There are comparatively less number of mineral deposits in the western part of Brazil. (2) Most of the western part of Brazil is covered by the Amazon river basin. There are evergreen dense rainforests in this areas. Due to dense forests this area has become inaccessible. As its effect, there are natural limitations on the use and exploitation of mineral resources available in this areas. (3) The density of human settlement is very low in the western part of Brazil. Thus, the demand for minerals in this part is comparatively low.

QUESTION SET 20 : ANSWER THE FOLLOWING ... 127 (4) Similarly, transport facilities are poorly developed in this areas. Therefore, mining has not developed in the western part of Brazil. (38) Write information about agriculture occupation in India. Ans. The information of agriculture in India can be given with the help of the following points : (1) Features : The features of agriculture in India are as follows : (1) Agriculture is one of the traditional occupations in India. (2) Nearly 60 per cent of land of India is under cultivation. (3) Most of the agriculture in India is of subsistence nature. (4) Compared to Brazil, the contribution of agriculture in Gross Domestic Product is high. (5) Compared to Brazil, the percentage of population of total population engaged in agriculture is high. (2) The factors promoting a strong base : Extensive plains, fertile soils, long growing seasons, variety in climate, etc. are the factors promoting a strong base for the development of agriculture in India. (3) Main crops grown : Rice, wheat, sorghum, millets, maize, etc. food crops, tea, coffee, cotton, sugarcane, rubber, jute, etc. cash crops and variety of spices, fruits and vegetables are grown on a large scale in India. (4) Foreign exchange : The agricultural produce like spices, mangoes, grapes, apples, vegetables, etc. are exported from India in world market. As its effect, agricultural produce helps in earning foreign exchange.
